column2: The former student Jamieson arrives for a visit with ideas as cracked as ever and tries to drum up interest in nudist weekends; Wunsch flies into such a rage that he refuses to speak to him. Reported in Wunsch's letter to Evarts of May 6, 1944.

The first summer Art Institute (1944). Blair arrives early one June morning, dirty and tired after a night on the Southern Railway: seats taken in Washington, standing on the platform between cars in high heels across Virginia, soot from the coal-burning locomotive, a seat found after midnight in a cockroach-infested car, a two-hour wait in Salisbury. No one is waiting for her at the station except the Alberses, who have come to pick up a parcel; a woman from the train introduces Blair to Anni, they load everything into their old car and drive up the bumpy road — then leave again with the suitcases still in the trunk. New clothes and high-heeled shoes; rationed gasoline; a missing axle on the driver's side of the old station wagon; eight bumpy miles to Lee Hall; two desks and a daybed with springs but no mattress and no chairs in the studio; an icy shower; a mattress damp from the mist; a bare bulb; a bank of wet red clay in front of the open window Consequences: Her unauthorized change of cabin scrambled the room assignments; the following week she was given the job of putting them back in order — a good experience of the democratic process.

A review meeting meant to calm things down; the Student Moderator proposes that majority voting replace consensus when unanimity is impossible; a furious quarrel over this point. Consequences: The old-timers are confirmed in their conviction that the newcomers do not understand the community's principles.

Dreier accuses Radin of gossip, intrigue, communist plots, and an obsession with developing the students' brains rather than the whole person; Radin, furious, announces that he will not return in the fall and leaves with his wife several days before the end of the term, without any explanation to the officials. A “truculent” departure (Wunsch) several days before the end of the term. Consequences: Radin does not return in the fall of 1944.

The Kolisch group begins work on Schoenberg's String Quartet, Op. 7; the new summer students crowd into the dark hall of North Lodge, sitting on chairs and on the stairs to watch. All the lakeside buildings seem filled with music: cello, singing, piano. a dark hall; spectators sitting on chairs and stairs; cello, voice, and piano practice in every building Consequences: an atmosphere of musical ferment before the Art Institute

The Art Institute is to open the following week, bringing Gropius, Ozenfant, de Creeft, Jean Charlot — who has promised to paint frescoes on the foundation piers of the Studies Building — and some twenty more students to an already overflowing crowd. “two dozen more students”; Charlot promises frescoes on the foundation piers of the Studies Building Consequences: Dreier smiles: the institutes will bring fame and perhaps money

After a mock quarrel with a truck driver (who had tried to kiss them, and to whom Jeanne had made her little socialist speech on the TVA), the two girls hitchhike in raincoats, small suitcases in hand, Jeanne in a jaunty beret. A police car stops; two policemen, both smug and furious, question them: one asks Jeanne whether she is a virgin, then Barbara, who answers yes with a modest air and a touch of acid. raincoats, small suitcases, a beret; summer dust on the road; the truck driver roars off in a cloud of dust; Jeanne brandishes John H. Randall Jr.'s The Making of the Modern Mind Consequences: charged with “loitering”

Charged with “loitering” (a Southern euphemism for prostitution; according to Jeanne, a vice campaign with police quotas, linked to a nearby military base). Denied a telephone call, locked up for the night with several dozen women, Black women separated from white by steel plates. A girl of 14 or 15, clearly tubercular, spits blood on the floor; her older sister, thrown into the cell later, announces that she has made twenty dollars from soldiers and berates her younger sister. A schoolteacher from Tennessee, arrested in a hotel room with a soldier (for free), believes her life is ruined. At midnight, Barbara celebrates her 21st birthday; they read their books and sleep a little, curled up on the floor. segregation by steel plates; 20 dollars earned by the sister; coughing blood; Barbara's 21st birthday at midnight Consequences: a forced medical examination the next morning

Jeanne has to shout at a guard to keep his hands to himself. They explain to the young doctor that they are students at Black Mountain, returning from a visit to a teacher at Fisk and a night at the Highlander Folk School — instead of sympathy, outrage: in many Southern minds, Black Mountain and Highlander are outposts of the Red menace. The doctor is furious when they insist on reading the authorization for the examination before signing, holding up the line. The examination described as something out of Faulkner; he announces that Barbara is positive for gonorrhea. He gives her medication: five days later, reexamined in Asheville, the result is negative — making any accusation impossible. a sadistic examination; medication; a second, negative examination in Asheville 5 days later Consequences: a sentence made heavier by the gonorrhea report

Sitting on a bench while the judge disposes of fights and family quarrels, they realize that none of the defendants, neither they nor the prostitutes, has a lawyer. A woman reporter advises Jeanne to say first of all “I want a lawyer”; but before the judge, too shaken, they say nothing. The judge sees the gonorrhea report, launches into a long lecture on the Scottsboro case, and sentences them to sixty days in the workhouse. A lawyer, apparently sent by the reporter, rushes in and promises to contact the college. 60 days in the workhouse; a lecture on Scottsboro; a calm, kind lawyer Consequences: transfer to the county penitentiary

A formidable police chief, his shortwave radio tuned to crime news from California, asks them among other things what they think of Black people (Jeanne, a real coward, she says, falls back on the Bible). Fingerprinting: Jeanne cries, and the photographer has to wait for her to dry her eyes. They may write letters, but censored ones: they write that they are in the hands of “friends of Dr. Straus,” to smuggle out the message racist fascists. a shortwave radio; censored letters; the code “friends of Dr. Straus” Consequences: Dreier alerted by the lawyer

48 hours after their imprisonment, Dreier arrives in Chattanooga and calls the judge, who reprimands him for the impropriety and calls the girls a couple of prostitutes. With the lawyer, and the promise to take them out of town immediately, the sentences are suspended. A return by bus, Dreier formal and polite, without a sermon (they did not like him much, he did not like them, no one could risk frankness). sentences suspended; a return by bus; the judge calls the girls prostitutes Consequences: a return to the college in disgrace

The Chattanooga newspaper publishes a fairly prominent article (because of the judge's lecture on Scottsboro) naming Black Mountain College; someone sends it to the Asheville Citizen, but the associate editor, favorable to the college, calls Wunsch, who explains everything and persuades him not to reprint the article. Consequences: a scandal contained locally

On the day the girls return, a special meeting: the affair rekindles the antagonisms that had lain dormant since the compromise on admitting Black students. Straus is indignant that the affair is being minimized and accuses Fran de Graaff, the girls' adviser, of having tolerated hitchhiking; she replies that she warned the girls, that no clear procedure existed between terms, and feels offended. A committee is formed: Dreier, Wunsch, Jalowetz, Straus, and Sam Brown (student moderator). a 5-member committee Consequences: a recommendation that Andy be excluded for the summer

Andy at first refuses to leave: she has nowhere to go and is indignant that Dreier questions her about her sex life, taking for granted that she had gonorrhea and wanting to hide the “fact” from the rest of the faculty. When Andy and her boyfriend Addison Bray “confess” to having had relations, Dreier lectures them on the image of respectability the college needs in its surroundings. it was worse than jail, says Andy; confessions of sexual relations Consequences: Andy and Addison leave

The faculty votes to accept the committee's recommendation (exclusion for the summer, free to return in the fall, so that the air may clear). Fran de Graaff's defense (Andy has done nothing dishonest) against Wunsch and Dreier (protect the college), Molly Gregory (if she stays she will be a hero or a martyr; let her take the consequences), Anni Albers (Andy seems frivolous and amused, says it was the best experience of her life). Josef Albers declares that thinking she is suffering deeply creates a serious problem for the college. Addison Bray announces that he is leaving too, furious at Dreier's Boy Scout interrogations; he obtains a leave. Andy persuades Jeanne to stay for the music institute (Jeanne will feel like a coward). They leave for Clark Foreman's summer house, about 60 miles away. 60 miles to the Foremans' Consequences: the start of a string of departures

A ten-week summer institute organized by Jalowetz, the college's music director, with a double aim: to spread the performance practice of the Second Viennese School and to celebrate Schoenberg's 70th birthday. Émigrés from the Schoenberg network gathered at Black Mountain — with the Blue Ridge in place of the Alps — form its core. Steuermann (Schoenberg's chosen pianist, New York) and Kolisch (violinist, founder of the Kolisch Quartet, on tour with the Pro Arte Quartet) are the most active; Krenek, in exile in the United States since 1938, gives a series of lectures, including “Arnold Schoenberg at Seventy”. Ten weeks of seminars, lectures, rehearsals, and concerts; Schoenberg, in poor health, declines the invitation Consequences: A fleeting re-creation of the Viennese Verein in North Carolina

After a grueling night on the train, no one at the station except the Alberses, who have come for a parcel; a bumpy ride, suitcases forgotten in the trunk; an icy shower; in the evening, a doorless station wagon to Lee Hall, a night climb to the cabins, a soaked mattress, an unauthorized change of room. Words: A woman from the train introduces Blair to Anni Albers. Atmosphere: Exhaustion, mist, red clay, warm dilapidation. Stakes: A rite of passage: physical discomfort against the intellectual dazzlement to come.

The Student Moderator proposes majority voting when consensus fails; a furious quarrel; Wunsch will say that a silent observer would have thought it a matter of life and death. Words: Wunsch: looking with calm eyes at the storm once it had passed; the observer would have thought it a matter of life and death, not a point of policy Atmosphere: Extreme passion over a question of procedure Stakes: Real power in the community: the old guard against the new

A car door slammed in feigned anger, a truck roaring off in the dust, Jeanne brandishing her Randall, thumbs raised, a police car growing larger in 4-5 tight shots, the policemen's questions (are you a virgin?), Andy's acidly modest answers, Jeanne's stifled giggles Words: “I don't think that's any of your business”; “Maybe your friend will. Are you a virgin?” — “Yes” (with perceptible acid) Atmosphere: summer dust, sun, the girls' insolence in the face of police arrogance Stakes: the tipping from carefree freedom into the Southern prison machine
Atmosphere: dark, carnivalesque, and terrifying Stakes: coming of age in jail

Straus's accusations, de Graaff's defense, Gregory's logic, Anni Albers's jab, a remark by Josef Albers that tips the balance, the vote to exclude, Bray's announced departure Words: paraphrased: Albers — thinking she is suffering in secret creates a serious problem for the college; Gregory — she will be a hero or a martyr Atmosphere: stifling, moralizing, hidden stakes Stakes: a minor incident turned into a major explosion

Foreman leaves to work for the CIO Committee for Political Action to get Roosevelt and a Democratic Congress reelected, leaving the college in a pretty bad hole (Dreier), since he had promised to raise funds during the summer; Bentley, proving his commitment to integration, teaches at Fisk for the summer. Consequences: A fund-raiser lost for the summer.

Two women students who venerate Bentley, with no hero on campus and far from home, notify their adviser de Graaff and head north to join Bentley at Fisk. Two twenty-year-old women students. Consequences: A week later, a Chattanooga lawyer calls Dreier about them.

Ten faculty members sign a terse statement: they no longer trust her to support the kind of education they believe in. Dreier, in a remarkably vague letter to Clark Foreman, accuses her and Bentley of being responsible for the students' increasingly immature and irresponsible attitude, of coddling their protégés instead of making them grow up. Fran refuses to resign: let them define the charges and formally request her resignation. 10 signers; a letter to Clark Foreman during his absence Consequences: three weeks of Board of Fellows meetings; an open split

Three weeks of Board of Fellows meetings; an attempt is made to hide the family quarrel from the summer institute people, who see Black Mountain as a Garden of Eden — but the two factions sit on either side of the dining hall and walk on opposite sides of the road to avoid each other. De Creeft, a summer member fond of people on both sides, has the idea of a mediation (continued beyond the passage). 3 weeks; factions separated in the dining hall and on the roads Consequences: impossible to hide; exodus or purge under way
At the meeting of July 17, 1944, de Graaff suggests that many of the college's women students are not virgins; Hansgirg nearly faints. De Graaff's account (telephone interview of December 10, 1967).
De Graaff maintains that she warned the girls against hitchhiking; Andy and Jeanne, as far as they remember, confirm her version. Telephone interview of December 10, 1967; interview of May 31, 1967.

Dreier sips his coffee, listening to Jalo and Cohen describe the arrival of the musicians; in the dark hall of North Lodge, the crowded students watch the Kolisch Quartet work on Schoenberg; Dreier finally smiles — the telephone rings: a Chattanooga lawyer, about Anderson and Wacker; Dreier feels he should never have smiled. Atmosphere: Musical euphoria abruptly shattered; an unforeseeable telephone call Stakes: The hope of renewal through the institutes against the legal crisis on its way

Two women students come back from Highlander and Fisk hitchhiking; a rumor of gonorrhea; Lowinsky and Anni Albers are indignant at de Graaff's irresponsibility; Hansgirg nearly faints; faculty meetings on July 10, 14, and 17; Dreier writes that even false publicity made action inevitable. Words: Bentley: “she didn't have it . . . there wasn't any gonorrhea around Black Mountain” Atmosphere: Rumor, indignation, moral vertigo Stakes: A young woman's reputation against the college's reputation

The players work on Schoenberg's Quartet, Op. 7, before the audience; the score scrolls on the suspended screen; disagreements over a phrase, discussions, real explanations, hard and concentrated work; little by little order emerges from the growing familiarity. Words: Wunsch to Evarts: “It was a privilege”; he speaks of disagreements, real explanations, hard and concentrated work, a dramatic adventure in which order is born of work. Atmosphere: Creative tension, concentration, an intellectual adventure in the heart of summer Stakes: Music as a model of democracy and of cultural reconstruction in wartime

Various letters of resignation reach the Board, which answers them pro forma; Kurtz writes on behalf of the Board to de Graaff on September 13, 1944, with a check for 1,000 dollars. $1,000. Consequences: The split consummated.

A signed statement dated August 13; Wunsch's statement of August 15; a letter from John Swackhamer to the college on August 21; Wunsch to Evarts on August 23, September 1, October 18; Evarts's reply on September 25; Wunsch reports the Cohens' reactions and mentions Kurtz and Dreier, weariness and depression (letter to Forbes of December 7, 1944). Consequences: Wunsch's exhaustion; he will eventually leave.

At the start of the fall 1944 term, Lowinsky raises integration at a faculty meeting; nearly a year of debate follows (accreditation, local reaction; a student or a teacher? how many, of which sex?). Straus and Kurtz oppose it. Lowinsky is mandated to make soundings, starting with Dr. George Redd, a sociologist at Fisk University who had already visited, who opens to him the network of Black colleges in the South. Straus, on research leave at Johns Hopkins, will in fact never return. Consequences: May 1945: the formula adopted — two Black students for the summer institutes, then a Black teacher in the fall if people of adequate caliber are available

The 1944 Music Institute brings together almost the whole circle of Schoenberg's students and admirers in the United States; Schoenberg, past seventy and living in Los Angeles, feels unable to make the long journey and sends Jalowetz (“Jalo”) a warm personal greeting for the opening. a letter from eight summer students to Wunsch, Sept. 14, 1944; financial estimates signed by Frederic Cohen; Lowinsky's speech, April 10, 1956 Consequences: Great joy for Jalowetz
Janis selects him for “Abstract and Surrealist Art in America” and publishes the book of the same title.

Those who left are preparing a new college: no work program, centered on the arts, with adviser-trustees, and seeking to train politicians among others (Wunsch to Forbes, December 7, 1944); Cohen tries to package a Music Institute (letters from Milton Rose to Dreier and to Gordon Chalmers, president of Kenyon College, March 1945). Consequences: The project does not supplant BMC.

After the Mondrian retrospective and the Stuart Davis exhibition at MoMA in 1945, intrigued by the energy, aggressiveness, and a kind of lyrical inevitability in Davis's paintings, she goes back several times to take notes and writes a twenty-page essay, frugally typed on both sides of the paper, not intended for publication, to clarify her thinking; Bill and Denby praise it, Thomson is impressed; twelve years later she publishes it almost unchanged in ARTnews and receives a note of thanks from Davis 20 pages, typed on both sides of the sheet

After a hideous review in Time, the St. Albans schoolboy walks down the hill to buy Miller's book at Franz Bader's. The book published in 1944 Consequences: The beginning of Williams's admiration for Miller
Venegas stops teaching the course in architectonic composition, conducted on the classical Beaux-Arts model since the School's founding in 1894. Consequences: An opening to modernist reform.

Harriett Engelhardt, a former student of Anni's at BMC, dies in 1945 while working for the Red Cross in Germany; her mother suggests a fund in her memory. Anni assembles a considerable collection of textiles, mainly from the Americas, exhibited at BMC and used as teaching material. Consequences: The collection later acquired by Yale

The college accepts its first Black students, the first “biracial” institution in the South of the United States; still a symbolic gesture according to Lane, but an early one. Lane speaks of a “token gesture, but one made early” Consequences: A pioneering position in the segregated South

During the 1945 summer session, Emma Hoffmann paints in oil the Hayes daughter, Africa, and Mrs. Hayes; Hayes's concert, a small voice of great emotional power, holds spellbound an audience drawn from every walk of life.

“Report from the Academy: The Experimental College,” Partisan Review, vol. 12, no. 3, 1945: after hearing Eliot advise young writers to avoid the academy (to work, for instance, in insurance, like Wallace Stevens), Bentley notes that most reputable American poets are teachers; disappointed by American higher education, he has chosen experimental reform. vol. 12, no. 3, 1945 Consequences: A reflection on the function of the experimental college.
Latest news: about forty students; a group of former members in New York is thinking of trying the experiment again elsewhere. about 40 students
The question of admitting Black students is settled in the affirmative only in the fall of 1945.

Preparing for parties: a day in the woodworking shop making improvised tableware — grapefruit plates, shallow rings turned from six-inch squares of mahogany, delicate three-tined forks, little butter knives from the wood of an old walnut tree, turned, sanded, and oiled. six-inch squares of mahogany; wood from an old walnut tree

A mountain cloudburst makes the creek overflow its banks; Lilly wakes her daughter, a human chain forms to evacuate the cook and his family from their cabin, the water up to their knees. The waters recede quickly, the cook's clothes are ruined, a collection is organized. Water up to the knees; clothes destroyed; a collection of donations Consequences: A collection to buy the cook new clothes

Out walking with the Bodkys, Roland Hayes spots a rattlesnake coiled behind a tall clump of grass, picks up a stone, and kills it with a throw of deadly accuracy. The cook skins the snake and prepares it for Erwin Bodky's supper. A stone thrown; the snake skinned and cooked; it tastes like chicken

On a night when the full moon floods the valley, a group walks along the dusty road to the waterfall and its slippery rock pool; everyone swims naked, the bravest under the falls, then they dry off by dancing before walking home at dawn, warmed by the walk. Icy water, chattering teeth, ghostly white bodies, farm dogs barking in the distance, a return at dawn

Festive Saturday evening concerts with leading European and American artists before students, teachers, and visitors from Asheville; everyone dresses up a little. Moments cited: Carol Brice in Brahms's Vier ernste Gesänge; Bodky and Heinitz in Beethoven's Sonata in A Major for cello and piano, with total silence between the movements. A dressed-up audience; one could have heard a pin drop between the movements

In a few terrible days, while he is rector of the college, Wunsch's homosexuality is explosively revealed. Consequences: His life ruined; the college's claim to an exceptional humanity seriously compromised.

Nine new teachers hired in the fall of 1945, eight of them young Americans with children. Enrollment up slightly to sixty students (only 25% boys). The college is officially approved for the GI Bill in music, English, social sciences, mathematics, and (if the equipment improves) chemistry. Percy Baker, a Black biologist from Virginia State College, hired as a mere visiting lecturer for the fall term of 1945 in keeping with the policy of racial recruitment. 60 students, 25% men; GI Bill approval Consequences: A new Board of Fellows policy: a first appointment always on trial for one year, then renewals for one, two, three, and five years.

According to the agreement with the Board of Fellows, Wunsch waits until one in the morning to come back for his belongings, then leaves for good before the community wakes, with no embrace and no word of farewell, in his little roadster. Yet only the day before he had been the college's titular head. 1 a.m.; “those little feet go back and forth” carrying books; the same little roadster as usual Consequences: Wunsch disappears for good from the life of the college

Molly Gregory, the ranking officer after Dreier's departure on vacation at Lake George, defies the faculty's ban on disclosing the affair: she gathers the whole community, and Herbert Miller tells the truth about the arrest, presenting the departure as a fait accompli. No protest from the students or the elders about the fact or the manner of the departure. Dreier's vacation at Lake George Consequences: A false official version is put out afterward

Official statement: after years of work without vacation, Wunsch has suffered a slight nervous breakdown and thinks it best to resign in order to take a necessary rest. the phrase “slight nervous breakdown” Consequences: The arrest for homosexuality concealed

Wunsch first goes back to Louisiana, ill for several months with a bad jaw infection; once cured, he drives to California in his roadster and literally disappears: letters unanswered, visits put off — not out of anger at Black Mountain but from a feeling of having got what he deserved: punishment and anonymity. The only rumor: a clerk in a post office. roadster; jaw infection; supposed work as a postal clerk Consequences: Wunsch's self-effacement

Teaching at the University of Maryland and finishing his Harvard doctorate in psychology, Wallen first has his CV forwarded by the Harvard Appointment Bureau, then, after two days of reflecting on the traditionalism of the procedure, writes a personal letter asserting that the CV will never say who he is. 27; two years of teaching at Maryland; a wife and a baby Consequences: A manifesto-letter that will win the college over

Straus, on leave at Johns Hopkins, at first finds in the letter a great many platitudes loudly presented and expects the worst; he meets Wallen, is pleasantly surprised, judges him genuine and stubborn in discussion, and, after a second visit to the Wallens' home, firmly recommends hiring him. a modern apartment without fanaticism: prints of Frans Hals and Van Gogh plus a Picasso; his speaking voice sounds like a tenor, but he sings second bass Consequences: A decisive positive recommendation

The Wallens win the community over at once, except two of the most vocal faculty members (Wallen suspects Albers, who does not like psychology), who seize on a rumor from Allport's letter — discharge from the army for nervous instability — to delay the appointment; the rumor is checked with the army, found to be false, and Wallen receives a one-year contract. a rumor of nervous instability; a one-year contract Consequences: The Wallens arrive in the fall of 1945

Wallen, 28, trained at Harvard, is hired to teach psychology; his idealism takes the form of a wish to impose more order on the college, which deeply irritates Albers. Wallen is 28 in 1946, a Harvard graduate Consequences: The main source of the frictions of 1946

By the mid-1940s, every unusual object is labeled a “matière”: an inedible dinner, moldy leftovers, a pile of garbage, a cow pat. The students laugh about it, and some gently tease him. “You name it, and I'll make a matiére out of it” Consequences: A new habit of responding to everything in visual terms

In the mid-1940s, Albers inaugurates an independent basic painting course, which he will later take to Yale. Consequences: The course addresses figure and ground, the application of marks to articulate volume in space, and the interaction of colors.
The former painter in residence at the Bauhaus teaches an advanced course during the summer of 1945.

Bill Levi, a graduate of the University of Chicago, where he taught philosophy, joins the faculty among several new teachers during a modest postwar expansion. The GI Bill swells student numbers Consequences: His relations with Albers will be stormy (“prickly”)

In an interview, Albers defends his Graphic Tectonic series, executed in zinc lithography: compositions built of elements preferably produced by mechanical means, combined in a mechanically emphasized order Very clean lines, uniformly modulated, a sharp boundary between black and white
Albers approaches Ansel Adams about a summer course in 1945 and asks him whether he thinks Edward Weston would be interested; Adams declines but proposes Brett Weston and Paul Strand in his place

A small building of glass, concrete, and wood with two slanting glass walls for excellent acoustics, intended for music practice and study. Tall glass walls reflecting the surrounding woods, integration with nature Consequences: Featured by California Arts and Architecture in April 1949 in the photo essay “Minimum House: A Student Project”

Johnson, told about the college by Elaine Schmitt Urbain during a summer school at the Art Institute of Chicago, is accepted there with her for the summer of 1945 Consequences: The start of a decisive training that lasts until 1948

A recital by the African American tenor as part of the Summer Music Institute, before the largest audience ever gathered at the college; a program mixing classical arias and Black songs, applauded as one of the great moments in the college's history about 400 spectators, 30 to 40 of them African Americans, the audience overflowing onto the porch; program: operas by Monteverdi, Haydn, Mozart, Schubert, then Negro spirituals and Creole and Afro-Brazilian songs; an evening described as mild (“balmy”) Consequences: the absence of any hostile reaction reassures the college and speeds up the recruitment of Black students and teachers

Alma Stone Williams had been invited to the 1944 Summer Music Institute; Sylvesta Martin becomes the first full-time Black student in the spring of 1945, and Percy H. Baker the first full-time Black teacher in the fall Consequences: the first white college in the South to admit a Black student, a decade before Brown v. Board of Education
Wunsch is arrested for alleged “crimes against nature” and then leaves the college Consequences: the loss of one of the chief supporters of integration

In 1945, the college's rector is driven out after an affair (adultery, truncated note). In the 1940s, members were discouraged from promiscuity and homosexuals pressed to stay discreet; in the 1950s, sexual freedom becomes almost a selling point, homosexuality and extramarital relations more or less openly acknowledged — without sexism disappearing.

After the war, the college abandons its refusal of the expression of emotion in favor of a new valuing of creative writing as self-expression: the progressive educator is replaced by a poet, M.C. Richards, and the students are conceived as writers alongside the new teachers of creative writing. Consequences: A change in the teaching of writing at the college.

Close to finishing her degree, Asawa learns that she will not be able to do the student teaching required for her diploma because of her race. Her friend Elaine Schmitt persuades her to join her in North Carolina for the 1946 Black Mountain Summer Institute. Consequences: Asawa joins BMC in the summer of 1946; she draws relentlessly and flourishes in Albers's classes (matière studies, the exploration of line in her notebooks).

Paul Beidler, a former student of Frank Lloyd Wright, replaces Kocher in 1945 and shortly afterward designs and supervises the construction of a music studio. Consequences: Continuity of modern architecture at the college after Kocher
Discharged, he returns to Port Arthur and discovers that his family has meanwhile moved to Lafayette.

Stationed in San Diego in the Navy, Rauschenberg visits the Huntington Library and sees original oil paintings for the first time, notably Gainsborough's The Blue Boy, which he knew only from books and playing cards. The Blue Boy (ca. 1770), seen until then on playing cards; he says: “It was a total overdose”; “Oh my God, these are not cards!” Consequences: He realizes that one can be an artist; his whole career will flow from the link between the reproduced photographic image and the painted original.

After his honorable discharge from the Navy in 1945, he returns to Port Arthur, but his family has moved without telling him, to Lafayette (Louisiana), with his sister Janet (born April 23, 1936). an unannounced move to Lafayette, Louisiana Consequences: he leaves to work in Los Angeles

Rauschenberg serves as a neuropsychiatric technician in the hospital wards; he draws from it a lasting conviction about the thin line between mental health and madness. His recollection: he learned how small the difference is between sanity and insanity, and that a combination of the two is essential. Consequences: The author connects this experience with Breton's as a medical orderly at Saint-Dizier in 1916 — a parallel never studied, in his view.

Péret attacks the poets of the Resistance: their “honor” supposedly consists in ceasing to be poets and becoming advertising agents — fidelity to anticlericalism and to the Surrealist refusal of patriotic committed art. The phrase quoted (modified translation), in English: all things considered, the honor of these “poets” consists in ceasing to be poets in order to become advertising agents
The end of the war is joyfully celebrated by the many Europeans, the faculty, and the American students. Consequences: Theodore Rondthaler obtains the college's approval for GI Bill benefits.

During the war there arrive Frederic Cohen (cofounder of the Jooss Ballet with Kurt Jooss) and his wife Elsa Kahl (a dancer), Edward Lowinsky (musicologist), Max Wilhelm Dehn (geometry, from Frankfurt), Eric Bentley (history and theater), Molly Gregory (woodworking, a member of Bennington's first graduating class). After the war: John Wallen (psychology), M.C. Richards (reading and writing), Bill Levi (philosophy and social sciences), Natasha Goldowski (corrosion), Charlotte Schlesinger (composer and pianist), Trude Guermonprez (textile design, the Jalowetzes' daughter), Franziska Mayer (weaver, niece of Max and Toni Dehn).

Motherwell, who could not afford any other summer destination, teaches at Black Mountain; among his students: Rauschenberg, Cy Twombly, Francine Gray. He remembers above all the Sunday baseball games. Baseball on Sundays

The Feiningers describe their impression of the site: high in the mountains, on the shore of a small lake in a broad valley, surrounded by wooded ranges; the magical mornings, with vapors rising from the lake and mists slowly revealing the outlines of trees and mountains. “the very element of light appearing as something mysterious and new”

Goodman notes in a footnote that the phrase about conscientious objectors as the finest types of people in the prisons is quoted from a private remark by the warden of the Danbury penitentiary, dated 1945. Note 17: the phrase is quoted from a private remark by the warden of the Danbury penitentiary (1945).

A footnote: a line of the poem comes from a private remark by the warden of the Danbury penitentiary in 1945 (his friends do not disapprove of the law and the judges, only of the jails). “My friends don't disapprove of the law and the judges, only the jails”

The college benefits from a cohort of talented veterans paid for by the GI Bill — cash payments with almost no conditions for tuition and living expenses — to attend this unaccredited, art-centered college. Consequences: The creative postwar years at the college
Publishes “Constructing Textiles” in the bulletin of the college's Summer Art Institute, reprinted in Design in April 1946

Rice realizes his old dream of returning to his native South Carolina. George Grice, president of the College of Charleston and an old acquaintance from the academic lecture circuit, finds him an old country house at a modest rent, available for a year while the owners are away. Big fireplaces, wide porches; a hardworking and interesting Black family farther down the road Consequences: Rice feels in his element.

Bob Wunsch left Black Mountain abruptly after being arrested in Asheville for homosexual acts with a marine. Josef Albers was elected rector of the college shortly afterward. Consequences: Albers becomes rector.

After the decommissioning of his last ship in San Francisco, Paul Jobs bets a friend that he will find a wife within two weeks; he marries Clara Hagopian, from an Armenian family that fled the Turks, raised in New Jersey. the bet: two weeks

Excited by the Stuart Davis exhibition at MoMA, before ever having published anything on art, Elaine writes for a month to clarify the works in her mind and finishes a ten-page article, which she drops into Edwin Denby's mailbox. The next day, a one-word telegram: “Magnificent”. She puts the article away without looking at it for about twelve years, until the Davis retrospective at the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis, when Thomas B. Hess asks her to update it. A ten-page article; a one-word telegram: “Magnificent”; about twelve years forgotten; published as “Stuart Davis: True to Life” (1957); a fan letter from the artist. Consequences: The revised article becomes “Stuart Davis: True to Life,” included in the collection.

Breton writes that here is an entirely new art, the culmination of twenty years of Gorky's patient and rugged development; Gorky's first admirers regard him as a newcomer. A quotation from Breton in 1945. Consequences: Breton among the first to give Gorky a just appreciation in print.
Julien Levy becomes his dealer; the Surrealists, in the person of André Breton, formally recognize him — a fact from which he draws great satisfaction.

After six months of planning, Foreman (very upset and ashamed, according to Fran de Graaff) announces one evening that he is becoming secretary of the National Citizens Political Action Committee. A hard blow for the Cohens, who have no money in reserve. 6 months of preparations Consequences: Fritz tries in vain to sell his Music Institute to other schools; the Cohens live in terrible poverty (Barbara Anderson) until he is hired as head of the Juilliard Opera Workshop

After lunch, Kazin sits alone at the top of the steps and plays the finale of Act II of The Marriage of Figaro, every day, eyes closed, face in the sun. The witness slips in through the back of the Round House every day to watch; at first incomprehension, then wonder, then listening: the sextet becomes the first music he truly hears. Atmosphere: a sunny, peaceful interlude, the sounds of mingled voices drifting over the still lake, Kazin's total concentration Stakes: the secret birth of a musical perception; an education through furtive observation

The paintings lined up against the wall; Albers, pointer in hand, designates a painting and asks theatrically; the audience shouts YES or NO in chorus. Words: “Does this have color?” — shouts of “YES!” or “NO!” Atmosphere: Choral fervor, Albers's dramatics, learning with the whole body. Stakes: Making people feel that color is relation, not vividness.

Angie, crouching among the plants, dazed by the hot sun, suddenly sees a pair of snow-white sneakers on the red soil; her gaze travels up the sharp crease of pressed jeans to a white shirt and a broad smile; Andy introduces herself. Words: Andy introduces herself, a fellow New Englander. Atmosphere: Crushing heat, red dust, friendship at first sight. Stakes: The birth of a friendship that will outlive the college.

A nighttime downpour; Lilly shakes Angie: the creek is over its banks; everyone goes out; a human chain forms in knee-deep water to evacuate the cook and his family; the waters recede quickly; the clothes are lost, and a collection follows. Words: “The creek is over its banks”. Atmosphere: Nighttime urgency, knee-deep water, quick relief. Stakes: Community solidarity in the face of the elements.
